items.readable_text:
Content:
Suppose that [MATH: f(x)] is a differentiable function. The graph of the derivative [MATH: y=f'(x)] is given below. Can we determine the intervals on which [MATH: f(x)] is increasing or decreasing?

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/328c4d6691648c740789a4955e9649f3]

Content:
To solve this problem, we use the following theorem:

Content:
> A differentiable function [MATH: f(x)] is increasing on the interval [MATH: (a,b)] if the derivative [MATH: f'(x)] is positive for every value in [MATH: (a,b).]

Content:
We also have the following related theorem:

Content:
> A differentiable function [MATH: f(x)] is decreasing on the interval [MATH: (a,b)] if the derivative [MATH: f'(x)] is negative for every value in [MATH: (a,b).]

Content:
From the graph, we see that [MATH: f'(x) > 0] on the intervals
[MATH: (0,4), \quad (7,10), \quad (10,15).]

Content:
Also from the graph, we see that [MATH: f'(x) < 0] on the intervals

Content:
[MATH: (4,7), \quad (15, \infty).]

Content:
Therefore, [MATH: f(x)] is increasing for [MATH: x \in (0,4) \cup (7,10) \cup (10,15)] and decreasing for [MATH: x \in (4,7) \cup (15, \infty).]

The graph of [MATH: y=f'(x),] the derivative of [MATH: f(x),] is given below. Find all the values of [MATH: x] where the function [MATH: y=f(x)] is decreasing.

[IMG: /graphics/21a4b398840f1a1c023bb6a4f6be940d]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, we recall the following:

  • If [MATH: f'(x) = 0] for all [MATH: x \in (a,b),] then the slope of [MATH: f(x)] is equal to zero on [MATH: (a,b).]

  • If [MATH: f'(x) > 0] for all [MATH: x \in (a,b),] then the slope of [MATH: f(x)] is positive on [MATH: (a,b).]

  • If [MATH: f'(x) < 0] for all [MATH: x \in (a,b),] then the slope of [MATH: f(x)] is negative on [MATH: (a,b).]

From the above graph, we can see that [MATH: f'(x)] is negative on the intervals [MATH: (-5,-2),] [MATH: (0,2)] and [MATH: (5,\infty)\mathbin{:}]

Therefore, [MATH: f(x)] is decreasing when [MATH: x\in (-5,-2) \cup (0,2) \cup (5,\infty).]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Suppose that [MATH: f(x)] is a differentiable function. The graph of the derivative [MATH: y=f'(x)] is given below. Can we determine the intervals on which [MATH: f(x)] is increasing or decreasing?

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/328c4d6691648c740789a4955e9649f3]

Content:
To solve this problem, we use the following theorem:

Content:
> A differentiable function [MATH: f(x)] is increasing on the interval [MATH: (a,b)] if the derivative [MATH: f'(x)] is positive for every value in [MATH: (a,b).]

Content:
We also have the following related theorem:

Content:
> A differentiable function [MATH: f(x)] is decreasing on the interval [MATH: (a,b)] if the derivative [MATH: f'(x)] is negative for every value in [MATH: (a,b).]

Content:
From the graph, we see that [MATH: f'(x) > 0] on the intervals
[MATH: (0,4), \quad (7,10), \quad (10,15).]

Content:
Also from the graph, we see that [MATH: f'(x) < 0] on the intervals

Content:
[MATH: (4,7), \quad (15, \infty).]

Content:
Therefore, [MATH: f(x)] is increasing for [MATH: x \in (0,4) \cup (7,10) \cup (10,15)] and decreasing for [MATH: x \in (4,7) \cup (15, \infty).]

---

Item 2 — Example: Determining Increasing and Decreasing Intervals Given the Graph of a Derivative

The graph of [MATH: y=f'(x),] the derivative of [MATH: f(x),] is given below. Find all the values of [MATH: x] where the function [MATH: y=f(x)] is decreasing.

[IMG: /graphics/21a4b398840f1a1c023bb6a4f6be940d]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we recall the following:

- If [MATH: f'(x) = 0] for all [MATH: x \in (a,b),] then the slope of [MATH: f(x)] is equal to zero on [MATH: (a,b).]
- If [MATH: f'(x) > 0] for all [MATH: x \in (a,b),] then the slope of [MATH: f(x)] is positive on [MATH: (a,b).]
- If [MATH: f'(x) < 0] for all [MATH: x \in (a,b),] then the slope of [MATH: f(x)] is negative on [MATH: (a,b).]

From the above graph, we can see that [MATH: f'(x)] is negative on the intervals [MATH: (-5,-2),] [MATH: (0,2)] and [MATH: (5,\infty)\mathbin{:}]

[IMG: /graphics/563c18d94ba3384f2aa7c230663efb75]

Therefore, [MATH: f(x)] is decreasing when [MATH: x\in (-5,-2) \cup (0,2) \cup (5,\infty).]

Item 5 — Tutorial: Relative Extrema

Content:
Recall that we can use the first derivative test to identify the relative extrema of a continuous function [MATH: f(x)\mathbin{:}]

Content:
- [MATH: f(x)] has a relative maximum at [MATH: x=a] if [MATH: f'(x)] changes its sign from positive to negative around [MATH: x=a.]

[IMG: /graphics/cd5ea6cac13140964f716a24613346a6]

Content:
- [MATH: f(x)] has a relative minimum at [MATH: x=a] if [MATH: f'(x)] changes its sign from negative to positive around [MATH: x=a.]

[IMG: /graphics/41cdbeff0f98192f70a09364ce697ae3]

Content:
So, to determine the relative extrema of a function [MATH: f(x)] by looking at a graph of [MATH: f'(x),] we need to pay attention to the locations where [MATH: f'(x)] changes sign.

---
